article.title: Self-Propagating npm Worm Hits OpenAPI React Query Codegen Tool a Day After TeamPCP Arrests
article.summary: Ten malicious versions of the 150,000-weekly-download @7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen package deployed a self-propagating credential stealer, with researchers unable to confirm whether TeamPCP is responsible.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

A popular npm code-generation tool used by developers building TanStack React Query clients from OpenAPI specifications was compromised in a supply-chain attack that shipped ten malicious package versions in two publishing waves roughly twenty minutes apart, according to [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/openapi-react-query-codegen-npm-compromise) and [Aikido Security](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/popular-code-generator-for-tanstack-query-hit-by-supply-chain-worm). The affected package, `@7nohe/openapi-react-query-codegen`, draws roughly 150,000 weekly downloads, according to both outlets. The compromise surfaced on August 28, 2026, according to Socket and Aikido, roughly a day after Australian authorities [announced criminal charges against two men accused of running the TeamPCP hacking campaign](/article/2026-08/28-australia-charges-two-men-with-14-offenses-over-teampcps-supply-chain-hacking-spree-that-hit-trivy-litellm-and-github) — a coincidence in timing that neither security firm could explain.

## What We Know

- The malicious releases spanned versions `0.5.4`, `0.5.5`, `1.6.3`, `1.6.4`, `2.2.1`, `2.2.2`, `3.0.3`, `3.0.4`, and two pre-release builds tagged `0.0.0-365d4eb738d3146583431948d3ba6e27a32556be` and `0.0.0-ec7876d6c917dad516ba69bbfafc948b834bf0ab`, according to [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/openapi-react-query-codegen-npm-compromise), which is corroborated by [Aikido's](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/popular-code-generator-for-tanstack-query-hit-by-supply-chain-worm) identical version list.
- Socket reported that "all ten remain installable at the time of writing, and the `latest` tag still resolves to the malicious `3.0.4`," as of its report, according to [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/openapi-react-query-codegen-npm-compromise). Developers were advised to roll back to the last known-good release on each line — `0.5.3`, `1.6.2`, `2.2.0`, or `3.0.2` — according to both [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/openapi-react-query-codegen-npm-compromise) and [Aikido](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/popular-code-generator-for-tanstack-query-hit-by-supply-chain-worm).
- The malware validates and reuses "GitHub, npm, PyPI, RubyGems, and JFrog credentials" it finds on infected systems, according to [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/openapi-react-query-codegen-npm-compromise). Aikido separately found the payload conducting "credential theft across GitHub, npm, PyPI, RubyGems, AWS, Azure, GCP, HashiCorp Vault, Kubernetes" along with "filesystem scanning for 150+ credential patterns," according to [Aikido](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/popular-code-generator-for-tanstack-query-hit-by-supply-chain-worm).
- On compromised systems with GitHub access, the malware "rewrites the workflow and adds `.github/_index.js` through GitHub's Git object and commit APIs," then collects secrets that are "serialized into an environment variable and writes them to `res.txt` before uploading the file as an artifact," according to [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/openapi-react-query-codegen-npm-compromise). Socket also found "encrypted collection exfiltration through attacker-created public GitHub repositories" and poisoning of packages across "npm, JFrog, and RubyGems," according to [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/openapi-react-query-codegen-npm-compromise).
- Aikido's analysis found the payload also carrying "worm propagation to maintainer's other packages and repositories" and "destructive commands," according to [Aikido](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/popular-code-generator-for-tanstack-query-hit-by-supply-chain-worm). The malware identifies itself internally with the string "Trinitite: Sponsored by Preview 2 Effects," according to [Aikido](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/popular-code-generator-for-tanstack-query-hit-by-supply-chain-worm).
- Both firms compared the attack's self-propagating design to earlier campaigns without confirming a shared operator. Socket wrote that "the artifact overlaps materially with public descriptions of both the 2025 Shai-Hulud npm worm and the later Mini Shai-Hulud campaign," but cautioned that "behavioral overlap alone does not establish shared operators or campaign identity," according to [Socket](https://socket.dev/blog/openapi-react-query-codegen-npm-compromise).
- Aikido noted the timing relative to the TeamPCP arrests, writing "it has only been a day since we heard the news of TeamPCP members being arrested in Australia" before noting it had "detected a new TeamPCP-like malware." The firm stopped short of attributing the attack to the group, stating that "whether we are dealing with a copycat, an ex-member who escaped the arrests, or a completely separate threat actor remains unclear," according to [Aikido](https://www.aikido.dev/blog/popular-code-generator-for-tanstack-query-hit-by-supply-chain-worm).
- The prior Mini Shai-Hulud campaign that Socket referenced hit TanStack, Mistral AI, and UiPath in May 2026, compromising more than 170 npm and PyPI packages, as [The Machine Herald previously reported](/article/2026-05/18-mini-shai-hulud-worm-hits-tanstack-mistral-ai-and-uipath-compromising-170-npm-and-pypi-packages-with-518m-combined-downloads).

## What We Don't Know

- Neither Socket nor Aikido has confirmed who is behind the attack, and both explicitly declined to attribute it to TeamPCP despite tactical similarities.
- It is not publicly known how many developers or CI pipelines installed the malicious versions before removal, or whether npm has since pulled the affected releases.
- No CVE or GitHub Security Advisory identifier had been assigned to the compromise in either firm's reporting.

## Background

The compromise lands one day after the Australian Federal Police, FBI, and Western Australia Police Force [charged two Western Australian men with a combined 14 offenses](/article/2026-08/28-australia-charges-two-men-with-14-offenses-over-teampcps-supply-chain-hacking-spree-that-hit-trivy-litellm-and-github) over the TeamPCP campaign, which authorities said potentially compromised more than 1,000 organizations through attacks on developer tools including Trivy, LiteLLM, and TanStack packages. It also follows a May 2026 wave of Mini Shai-Hulud infections that [hit TanStack, Mistral AI, and UiPath](/article/2026-05/18-mini-shai-hulud-worm-hits-tanstack-mistral-ai-and-uipath-compromising-170-npm-and-pypi-packages-with-518m-combined-downloads) across more than 170 npm and PyPI packages.
